title: Sergius of Radonezh
hook: a Russian hermit in the forest who shared bread with a bear and founded a great monastery

segments.voice: Yesterday, the monks of Athos, praying in stillness for the light on the mountain, and your line was the light of tabor.

One piece of bread, on a tree stump at the edge of a clearing. Deep in a Russian forest, a young man has built a small wooden cell and a chapel with his own hands. No village nearby, no road worth the name. One day, the old account says, a bear comes out of the trees, hungry, and stands looking at him. He doesn't run. He brings out a piece of his bread and sets it on the stump. The bear eats it and goes away. Then it comes back, again and again. Today: Sergius of Radonezh.
screen: `ONE PIECE OF BREAD ON A STUMP.`
`A BEAR COMES OUT OF THE TREES.`

segments.voice: Sergius is a monk the Russian Orthodox Church honors as a saint, and his story comes down through a Life written by a monk named Epiphanius. As a young man, the Life says, Sergius went into the forest to live alone with God. He chopped his own wood, grew what he could, and prayed. And the bear kept coming. Here's the detail the Life lingers on. Some days Sergius had only one piece of bread, and on those days, the story goes, he gave it to the bear and went hungry himself, rather than send the animal away with nothing. An odd kind of holiness: not a sermon, but a crust, and an empty stomach. Other Christian stories, too, put holy people at peace with wild animals, and Mark's Gospel has a small line about Jesus in the desert, in the King James Bible: "and was with the wild beasts". In these stories the wilderness isn't only danger; it's also where creatures and a person at prayer learn to live side by side. Sergius didn't stay alone. Other monks heard of him and came to live near him, cells went up around his, and a community grew, dedicated to the Holy Trinity. The Life remembers him as a leader who still carried water, baked bread and wore patched clothes. A monastery grew where his cell had been. But the scene that stays is smaller: the stump, the bread, and the bear.

Think of an animal near your life, a pet on the couch, the birds outside, a neighbor's dog, and one small thing it could use: fresh water, a few seeds, a walk, or simply your patience. Sit with that creature in mind, the way Sergius sat at the edge of his clearing. If you pray, give thanks for it; if not, let it be in your thoughts, just as it is.
Sergius. A forest hermit of Radonezh honored by the Orthodox Church, who shared his bread with a bear and around whom a community of the Holy Trinity grew.
Your line: bread with the bear. Even when it was the last piece. Day eight hundred twenty-seven, in the books.

howItsDone: The Russian Orthodox Church honors Sergius of Radonezh as a saint, and the Trinity monastery that grew up around his forest cell bears his name; his story with the bear is told in his Life.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or counts used. The bear episode, the last-piece detail, the arrival of other monks, the Trinity dedication and his manual work are taken from Epiphanius's Life (as revised by Pachomius); confirm each is in the Life.
